newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan proposes brief renewal of U.N. Angola force.
newsitem.headline: Annan proposes brief renewal of U.N. Angola force.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Monday he would recommend a two-month extension of the U.N. peacekeeping force in Angola if a delayed government of national unity were formed before the expiry of the force's current mandate at the end of February.

This was on the understanding that steps would be taken to transform it into a smaller, reconfigured U.N. observer mission that would remain until the end of 1997, he said in a written report to the Security Council.

But if former UNITA rebels designated to serve in the national unity government failed to arrive in Luanda, the capital, by Feb. 12 as currently scheduled, Annan said he would recommend the Security Council extend the mandate of the U.N. force for only one month, until March 31.
If by then the national unity government had still not been established, the Security Council "may wish to consider appropriate steps to address the situation," he added.

Formation of a government of national unity and reconciliation would come after repeatedly delayed efforts to implement an agreement between the Angolan government and UNITA that was signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in 1994, ending two decades of civil war in Angola.

Establishment of the government, scheduled for Jan. 25, was postponed after negotiations failed to find an acceptable role for UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, who still controls much of Angola, including diamond-rich areas.

The U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM III), which has been helping oversee the peace accord, comprised 6,638 troops, military observers and civilian police from more than 30 countries on Feb. 1, after the withdrawal of about 650 troops at the end of 1996.

The U.N. force has been monitoring such elements of the agreement as the assembling and disarming of UNITA fighters in so-called quartering areas and the incorporation of some of them into a new Angolan army.
But Annan said the "pace of implementation of the remaining military and political tasks, owing mainly to the lack of cooperation of UNITA, has, once again, been painfully slow and disappointing."
Of the 70,660 UNITA troops registered in quartering areas by Feb. 1, more than 22,600 had deserted or were temporarily absent from U.N. camps, he said.

Only 5,895 UNITA officers and men had actually been incorporated into the Angolan army by the beginning of this month and it was increasingly unlikely that it would be possible to select 26,300 as originally planned.

Annan did not say how many troops would be required for the proposed U.N. follow-on mission. As well as carrying out military tasks, he said it should focus on political, police and human rights aspects, humanitarian activities and public information programmes.

"The main emphasis of the mission should be on peace consolidation, confidence-building and national reconciliation, with a view to creating an environment conducive to long-term stability in the country," he added.
